title: Sold Out in Two Hours: How Indian Mangoes Became America's Most Coveted Summer Fruit
excerpt: From Costco shelves to embassy tasting events, Alphonso and Kesar mangoes are fuelling a $10 million export boom — and a wave of NRI nostalgia.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indian mango exports to the U.S. reached $10 million in 2023-24, growing 130% year-over-year.
  • Costco's Kesar mangoes sold out within two hours of arrival in major U.S. cities.
  • The U.S. mango import market is projected to exceed $1 billion in value by 2025.
  • Mango diplomacy is fostering cultural connections between India and the U.S. through this beloved fruit.
  • Premium subscription services for mango deliveries are emerging, with costs up to $2,000 for the season.

In the third week of May, Costco stocked Indian Kesar mangoes at stores in Greater Seattle, Las Vegas, New Jersey, and Greater Los Angeles. According to Costco representatives, every mango sold out within two hours of arriving on the shelves. Two hours. For a fruit that was banned from the United States until 2007. The Indian mango has become, improbably and unmistakably, one of America's most coveted summer foods — a luxury item that commands subscription passes costing up to $2,000 for weekly deliveries, sells out faster than concert tickets at major retailers, and has turned diaspora nostalgia into a $10 million annual export business that is growing at 130 per cent year over year. ## The Numbers Behind the Mania India is the world's largest producer of mangoes, with an annual output exceeding 26 million metric tonnes and more than 1,000 named varieties. Yet for 18 years — from 1989 to 2007 — Indian mangoes were banned from the American market over phytosanitary concerns. Since that ban was lifted, exports have surged. The value of Indian mango exports to the United States reached $10 million in the 2023-24 fiscal year, up 130 per cent from $4.36 million the previous year. U.S. mango imports overall are projected to grow by a further 7 per cent in 2026, and the total American mango import market crossed $1 billion in value in 2025. ![Las Vegas — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Las_Vegas_from_above_%2840064746644%29.jpg/3840px-Las_Vegas_from_above_%2840064746644%29.jpg) > **"Mango Import Market (Billion USD, 2025)

Projected U.S."** The varieties driving this demand read like a gazetteer of India's mango heartland: Alphonso from Maharashtra's Ratnagiri and Devgad, Kesar from Gujarat, Langra and Dussehri from Uttar Pradesh, Banganapalli and Himayat from Andhra Pradesh, and Rajapuri from Gujarat. ## Mango Diplomacy India's Ambassador to the United States, Vinay Kwatra, has a name for what is happening: "mango diplomacy." "We all have a sense of diaspora, particularly in the US — a sense of summer nostalgia," Kwatra told IANS ahead of a mango festival organised by the Embassy of India in Washington. "Summer vacations remind us of the times when we would enjoy mango and the deliciousness of this fruit to our heart's content. But we are now facing a very, very happy situation where this nostalgia is now available with American retailers." The Consulate General of India in Seattle recently hosted the second edition of "Mango Magic," a promotion and tasting event that brought together more than 100 importers, distributors, and senior representatives from major retailers, including Costco. Guests sampled seven premium varieties of Indian mangoes. The partnership with the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) underscores New Delhi's seriousness about the American market. In his Mann Ki Baat podcast, Prime Minister Narendra Modi himself praised India's mango farmers for "taking this journey from the village to the global market," highlighting the rich diversity from Maharashtra's Alphonso to Bihar's Zardalu. ## What It Means in the Desi Kitchen For the four million-plus Indian Americans in the United States, the arrival of Indian mangoes in mainstream retail stores is about something far deeper than fruit. It is about identity. ![Greater Los Angeles — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/45/Good_morning_LA_%28cropped%29.jpg)
Mangoes in American Retail
›Kesar mangoes sold out in two hours at Costco.
›Indian mangoes were banned in the U.S. until 2007.
›Mangoes now sit alongside strawberries and blueberries in stores.
›Premium subscription services for mangoes are emerging.
Every NRI family has a mango story. The uncle who packed a suitcase with Alphonsos from Mumbai. The grandmother who made aamras so thick it stood up on the plate. The summer holidays in India where mangoes were eaten by the dozen, juice running down arms, seeds sucked clean. For decades, that experience was impossible to replicate in America. Indian grocery stores stocked mangoes from Mexico and Brazil — perfectly fine fruit, but to a palate raised on Alphonso, about as similar as a Granny Smith is to a Fuji. The real thing arrived occasionally, in limited quantities, at eye-watering prices, and disappeared before most families could get to the store. Now, Kesar mangoes sit in the same Costco refrigerators as strawberries and blueberries. The shift is seismic. ## The Business of Nostalgia The supply chain that makes this possible is genuinely complex. Indian mangoes must be irradiated before export (a requirement that drove the original ban), and the fruit's short season — roughly March through July — creates a narrow window for air-freighted shipments. Rising freight costs and tariff uncertainty have pushed prices higher, but demand has proven remarkably resistant to cost. Premium subscription services have emerged to meet the most devoted buyers. Some offer weekly deliveries of curated mango boxes throughout the season, with premium tiers reaching $2,000 for the full run. It is a business model that treats a fruit the way wine clubs treat Napa Cabernet — as a luxury worth paying for, season after season. The consul general in Seattle, Prakash Gupta, linked the moment to what he called a historical precedent: during President George W. Bush's 2006 visit to India, Bush tasted an Alphonso and reportedly declared, "What a hell of a fruit." "That started that wave of mangoes coming into the US," Gupta said. Twenty years later, the wave has become a flood. And for Indian Americans who spent years chasing the taste of home, every Costco checkout is a small, sweet victory.
